newsitem.title: GERMANY: F.O. LICHT - Daily sugar report.
newsitem.headline: F.O. LICHT - Daily sugar report.

text.p: The following is a direct contribution from statistician F.O. Licht in Ratzeburg, Germany. Please address any queries to Helmut Ahlfeld on +00 49 4541 88920.

White sugar futures in London felt continuing pressure on nearby values from mixed sellers after a lacklustre raws performance failed to inspire an upturn in sentiment. December shed $1.10 to close at $308 while March was 50 cents down at $305. The white sugar market in Paris was closed on Friday for All Saints Day. In New York raw sugar futures closed unchanged to higher with spot March gaining 6 points to close at 10.36 cents/lb. May was up 2 points at 10.46 cents/lb. Market sources said prices are oversold and put resistance at around 10.56 cents/lb in March. However others said that bearish fundamentals will continue to weigh on prices.

Thailand - Thailand exported 4.36 million tonnes of sugar, raw value in January/September 1996, up from 3.678 million in the same period in 1995. Total exports in calendar 1995 rose sharply to 3.9 million tonnes from 2.7 million the previous year. Main destinations in January/September were Japan (695,965 tonnes vs 488,951 tonnes), Indonesia (644,360 vs 307,000 tonnes) and South Korea (365,600 vs 270,994 tonnes). China, the biggest buyer last year, took 448,743 tonnes in January/September 1996 which compares to 1.411 million tonnes the same period in 1995.

MALAYSIA - Sugar imports in July 1996 amounted to 105,700 tonnes raw value, down from last year's 113,250. This brought cumulative imports in the first seven months of 1996, January/July, to 609,167 tonnes against 571,911. Total imports in calendar 1995 reached 1.03 million tonnes, up from 959,518 in 1994. Major countries of origin in January/July 1996 were Thailand with 366,600 tonnes raws, up from 249,565, Australia with 217,567 tonnes compared to 265,280 and South Africa with 25,000 tonnes against nil. Sugar exports reached 10,773 tonnes up from last year's 9,375 tonnes. This brought cumulative exports in January/July 1996 to 65,957 tonnes compared to 58,037 in the like period the previous year. Total 1995 exports reached 123,561 tonnes, down from 159,525 in 1994. Major countries of destination in January/July 1996 were Singapore with 39,334 tonnes whites, Indonesia with 15,728 tonnes and the Philippines with 4,236 tonnes.

JAPAN - Sugar imports hit a new low in 1995/96 (October/September). Imports in September 1996 reached a mere 102,311 tonnes, raw value, down from last year's 126,653 tonnes. This brought total imports in 1995/96 to 1.68 million tonnes, down on last year's 1.71 million tonnes and 1993/94 result of 1.70 million. Major countries of origin in October/September 1995/96 were Thailand with 748,179 tonnes raws against 583,415 tonnes, Australia with 596,766 tonnes compared to 761,485 tonnes, South Africa with 193,737 tonnes, up from 46,922 and Cuba with 110,601 tonnes against 193,573 tonnes. Sugar exports in 1995/96 amounted to 4,699 tonnes against 1,436 tonnes 1994/95. The major country of destination 1995/96 was China with 2,168 tonnes whites against 29 tonnes.

RUSSIA - Russian sugar imports lost some of their impetus in the third quarter of 1996. Total imports in July/September 1996 amounted to 568,000 tonnes raw value, down from last year's 986,000. However, cumulative imports are still considerably up on last year, reaching 2.93 million tonnes in January/September 1996, from 2.35 million in the like period the previous year. Major countries of origin in January/September 1996 were Cuba with 1.15 million tonnes raws against 507,400 tonnes, Ukraine with 1.06 million tonnes whites compared to 934,299 and Brazil with 189,800 tonnes raws and 29,000 tonnes whites against 54,000 tonnes whites in January/September 1995.

Iran bought three cargoes of Thai and EU-origin white sugar for shipment in February. It bought one Thai cargo at $322 per tonne fob, and two EU cargoes at $318 and $317 per tonne. Physical brokers said the purchases were made at relatively low prices and formed a part of Iran's regular buying programme at this time of year.
